A linear mixed model found no significant difference in the predictive value of the better compared to the worse eye for questionnaire scores (β = 2.14, SE = 4.88, p = 0.35). There was no significant correlation between EQ-VAS scores and VFQ-25 or LLQ findings (ρ ≈ 0, p > 0.90). CONCLUSIONS: Microperimetry is a patient-relevant measure in inherited retinal diseases. This study demonstrates to stakeholders, such as regulatory bodies, how visual function measures translate to patients' quality-of-life. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER AND REGISTRATION DATE: ISRCTN24016133 ( http://www.isrctn.org/) , 17 August 2022.
42970243.authors: Raji S, Taylor LJ, MacLaren RE
42970243.journal: Ophthalmic & physiological optics : the journal of the British College of Ophthalmic Opticians (Optometrists)
42970243.title: Association Between Quality of Life and Visual Function in Inherited Retinal Disease: A Cross-sectional Study in a Retinal Genetics Centre.

42971418.abstract: Cell-cycle regulatory perturbations are increasingly implicated in retinal degeneration, yet their biological significance varies fundamentally across retinal cell types because proliferative competence differs between terminally differentiated neurons and proliferation-capable retinal populations. While retinal neurons normally maintain permanent cell-cycle exit, Müller glia, microglia, retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, endothelial cells, and pericytes retain varying capacities for quiescence, proliferation, and injury-induced reactivation. Consequently, alterations in cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), RB-E2F signaling, DNA replication machinery, or checkpoint regulators may represent distinct biological states depending on cellular context. In this review, we examine cell-cycle perturbations across inherited retinal diseases (IRDs), age-related macular degeneration (AMD), diabetic retinopathy (DR), retinal gliosis and inflammation, and retinal organoid models. We critically assess current evidence for neuronal cell-cycle re-entry and propose a practical evidence hierarchy that distinguishes pathway activation, neuronal localization, progression through cell-cycle phases, cell-type-specific causality, and longitudinal cellular fate. We argue that many reported findings reflect incomplete or ambiguous evidence and should not be equated with bona fide neuronal cell-cycle re-entry. We further propose a fate-bifurcation model in which cellular outcomes are determined by the depth and duration of cell-cycle engagement together with cell identity, checkpoint integrity, CDK inhibitor activity, DNA damage burden, metabolic state, and microenvironment cues. Under this framework, limited or checkpoint-restrained engagement may support transient neuronal adaptation or survival, whereas sustained activation may promote senescence-like states, and deeper progression under inadequate checkpoint control may contribute to neuronal dysfunction and death. In proliferation-competent retinal compartments, related pathways may instead drive gliosis, immune expansion, epithelial remodeling, angiogenesis, or senescence. By integrating evidence across retinal diseases and cell types, this state-based framework provides a unified interpretation of apparently conflicting observations and offers a conceptual foundation for developing cell-type- and state-specific therapeutic strategies for retinal degeneration.
42971418.authors: Du W, Ma R, Hong Y et al.
42971418.title: Cell-cycle regulatory responses in retinal degeneration: From post-mitotic homeostasis to cell-state transitions and fate decisions.

42972018.abstract: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP), a leading cause of inherited blindness, results in a subset of cases from phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6) deficiency. We evaluated a novel gene therapy construct, AAV8-RK-PDE6B-3'UTR, in the rd10 mouse model which has a homozygous missense variant that disrupts the function of the β-subunit of PDE6. The construct utilises a rhodopsin-kinase promoter, human PDE6B cDNA, and a PDE6B 3' untranslated region (3'UTR), which was delivered subretinally at postnatal day 12 (P12). Treated mice showed sustained preservation of retinal function and structure for up to 15 months, as confirmed by visual acuity (VA), electroretinography (ERG), optical coherence tomography (OCT), and immunohistochemistry. This represents the longest functional and structural follow-up reported for AAV-mediated PDE6B gene supplementation in the rd10 model. Inclusion of the PDE6B 3'UTR increased PDE6B expression in vitro and improved functional rescue in four week post-therapy testing. These data indicate that the combination described here of vector capsid type and promoter specific to photoreceptors, along with PDE6B 3'UTR sequence may provide benefit in therapeutic effect in PDE6B gene therapy.
42972018.authors: Eamegdool SS, Loi TH, Sabri A et al.
42972018.title: AAV8-PDE6B with 3'UTR provides rescue of photoreceptor structure and function in the rd10 mouse model of retinitis pigmentosa.

42972392.abstract: Adhesion G protein-coupled receptor V1 (ADGRV1) is one of the largest and most modular receptors in the adhesion G protein-coupled receptor (aGPCR) family, integrating functions of cell adhesion, mechanosensing, and classical G protein signaling. Its structural domains, including calcium exchanger β (Calx-β) repeats, laminin G-like/ pentraxin (LamG/PTX) domain, epilepsy-associated (EPTP/EAR) repeats, GPCR-autoproteolysis-inducing (GAIN) domain/GPCR proteolytic site (GPS) module with tethered Stachel peptide, seven transmembrane (7TM) helices, and PDZ-binding motif (PBM), jointly shape its activation, intracellular transport, and effector coupling. Recent studies indicate that ADGRV1 exhibits context-dependent signaling, particularly through G protein coupling and ciliary localization, thereby influencing calcium homeostasis, autophagy, and developmental pathways. Genetic and functional evidence links ADGRV1 to Usher syndrome (USH) type II, epilepsy, and emerging associations with Alzheimer's disease (AD), and recurrent somatic alterations in diverse cancers. Variants in ADGRV1 modulate processes such as ankle-link complex (ALC) assembly, synaptic stability, amyloid and tau regulation, chemoresistance, and immune microenvironment remodeling. Despite this progress, many aspects of its signaling mechanisms, ligand interactions, and disease relevance remain poorly understood. Future work combining high-resolution structural studies, systematic mapping of signaling bias, and rigorous translational validation will be essential to clarify the multifaceted roles of ADGRV1 and to evaluate its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target. ADGRV1 is an unusually large protein found on the surface of many cells in the body. It acts like a sensor and communication hub, helping cells respond to their surroundings and send messages inside the cell. Because of its size and complex structure, ADGRV1 can perform several roles at once, including helping cells stick to each other, detect physical forces, and control internal signaling processes. Changes in the ADGRV1 have been linked to several human diseases, including Usher syndrome, which affects hearing and vision, certain forms of epilepsy, and possibly Alzheimer’s disease. Alterations in ADGRV1 have also been observed in some cancers. However, scientists still do not fully understand how changes in this single protein can lead to such different health problems.In this review, we have gathered the latest knowledge about how ADGRV1 is structured, how it is activated, and how it influences intracellular communication. Rather than focusing on only one pathway or disease, we look at the bigger picture and highlight common themes in how this protein works. We also discuss important unanswered questions and suggest directions for future research. A clearer understanding of ADGRV1 may help explain why it is involved in diverse diseases and could guide the development of new diagnostic tools or treatments in the future.
42972392.authors: Liu Q, Tian J, Xin L et al.
42972392.title: Structural features and disease-associated functions of ADGRV1: insights from signaling mechanisms.

42977211.abstract: BACKGROUND: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) represents a degenerative disorder of photoreceptors marked by reactive gliosis and inflammatory processes. This present work aimed to explore how apolipoprotein E (ApoE) influenced the retinal inflammation and to its potential mechanism involved in RP. METHODS: ApoE levels were measured by ELISA in serum from healthy volunteers and patients with RP and by western blotting in retinas from postnatal day 28 wild-type (WT) and rd10 (Pde6brd10) mice. Retinal inflammation was assessed via cytokine expression and reactive gliosis of glia cells based on RNA-seq, qPCR, and immunofluorescence. ApoE-knockout mouse was used to examine the effect of ApoE on the retinal inflammatory response. A co-culture system of a microglial cell line (BV2 cells) and a Müller glial cell line (QMMuC-1 cells) was established to simulate retinal inflammation in vitro and to explore the effect of ApoE on miR-146a/b and PU.1 expression. RESULTS: ApoE levels was increased in the serum of patients with RP and were mainly upregulated in Müller cells of rd10 mice. Reactive gliosis and inflammation were detected in rd10 mice and ApoE knockout mice. In vitro, activated BV2 cells induced ApoE expression in QMMuC-1 cells. ApoE treatment significantly repressed IL-1β and TNF-α expression in both cell types. Mechanistically, ApoE may promote miR-146a/b expression via PU.1, thereby regulating miR-146, critical negative regulators of NF-κB signaling. CONCLUSIONS: ApoE is compensatorily upregulated to inhibit retinal inflammation though miR-146a/b and may serve as a potential target for the clinical diagnosis and treatment of retinal degenerative disease.
42977211.authors: Gu B, Lu J, Jiang W et al.
42977211.title: ApoE is associated with retinal inflammation during the progression of retinitis pigmentosa.

42979557.abstract: Irreversible vision loss, affecting millions of people worldwide, most often ends in the death of retinal neurons that the human eye cannot replace. Across the tree of life, however, evolution has repeatedly produced strategies that address the core problems of vision restoration: zebrafish and salamanders regenerate functional retinas and lenses, and a wide range of species have tuned photoreceptors, optics, and neural circuits to extract maximal information from light. This review systematizes these biological strategies and evaluates how each is being translated toward human therapies, with grading of the strength of evidence behind every translational claim. We organize the field by biological strategy: regeneration, spectral tuning, low-light adaptation, high-acuity optics, polarization and additional channels, and neural processing, and for each trace the path from mechanism to therapy or device. The most mature translations are already clinical: gene therapy for inherited retinal disease, and optogenetic restoration of vision in blind patients. Regenerative approaches informed by regenerating species, including Müller glia reprogramming, ciliary marginal zone biology, retinal organoids, and stem cell transplantation, are advancing toward clinical feasibility. Spectral, low-light, and acuity specializations provide mechanistic blueprints and bio-inspired devices, though their biological translation to humans remains preclinical or theoretical. We conclude with the controversies, research gaps, and ethical considerations that will shape whether nature's strategies can be safely and equitably applied to restore human vision, and we briefly consider the evidence and limits of extending vision beyond its native range.
42979557.authors: Weener M, Khachatryan L, Baziyan B
42979557.title: What we can learn from nature to restore human vision.

42979679.abstract: PURPOSE: Retinitis pigmentosa is a collection of heritable retinal dystrophies, in which rod and cone photoreceptor cells of retina die gradually. This disorder can be classified into syndromic and non-syndromic forms. One of the most prevalent syndromic forms of retinitis pigmentosa is Bardet-Biedl syndrome. More than 24 genes have been reported in the pathogenesis of Bardet-Biedl syndrome. One of these genes is MKKS centrosomal shuttling protein. METHODS: Whole exome sequencing was applied to find the disease-associated variant in an Afghan patient from a consanguineous family living in Iran. This patient and her two brothers have Bardet-Biedl syndrome. Bioinformatics tools were utilized to assess the structural impact of the identified variant. The 3D structure of MKKS protein was predicted, and its model quality was evaluated. The variant was introduced into the wild type model and its structural effects were analyzed. RESULTS: Whole exome sequencing revealed a novel homozygous variant NM_170784.3 (MKKS): c.882A>C; p.(Gln294His), which is segregating with the disease phenotype in the pedigree. Structural modeling showed that this variant does not induce significant global conformational changes in the MKKS protein, but pointed to a possible local effect on the structure around that residue. CONCLUSIONS: This finding expands the variant spectrum of MKKS gene in patients with Bardet-Biedl syndrome in an understudied population.
42979679.authors: Kalhor H, Hooshmandi S, Ghofrani M
42979679.title: Identification of a novel homozygous variant in the MKKS gene in a consanguineous Afghan family with Bardet-Biedl syndrome living in Iran.

42980597.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate 3-year visual, refractive, and anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT)-measured intraocular lens (IOL) positional stability after anterior capsulorhexis optic capture (ACOC) in eyes with zonular insufficiency, with secondary assessment of capsulorhexis contraction in retinitis pigmentosa (RP). SETTING: University hospital, Japan. DESIGN: Retrospective case series. METHODS: Among 239 patients (311 eyes) undergoing ACOC, 7 eyes (2.3%) developed spontaneous loss of optic capture; these events were reported as safety events, and the primary longitudinal analysis included 304 eyes with maintained capture. Corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA), absolute refractive prediction error, IOL tilt and decentration, intraocular pressure (IOP), endothelial cell density (ECD) loss, complications, and capsulorhexis minor-axis ratio in RP eyes were assessed through 36 months. RESULTS: CDVA improved and stabilized after 3 months. Absolute refractive prediction error remained stable between 3 and 36 months (0.43-0.50 D). AS-OCT-measured IOL tilt and decentration remained stable from 3 to 36 months. In RP eyes, the minor-axis ratio was 0.92 ± 0.05 at 3 months and 0.96 ± 0.04 at 24 months, with no progression beyond 3 months. IOP at 36 months did not differ significantly from baseline, and ECD loss remained stable from 3 to 36 months. Capsular block syndrome (CBS) occurred in 218 eyes (71.7%); 210 underwent Nd:YAG posterior capsulotomy for CBS. Serious complications were infrequent. CONCLUSIONS: ACOC was associated with stable visual, refractive, and anatomical outcomes for up to 3 years in eyes with maintained optic capture. In high-risk RP eyes, progressive capsulorhexis contraction was not observed beyond 3 months.
42980597.authors: Mitooka S, Masuda Y, Komatsu K et al.
42980597.journal: Journal of cataract and refractive surgery
42980597.title: Anterior Capsulorhexis Optic Capture for Zonular Insufficiency: Three-Year Outcomes With a Retinitis Pigmentosa Subanalysis.

42982416.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Coats-like vasculopathy (CLV) presents with retinal telangiectasias and exudative retinopathy. Unlike classic Coats disease, CLV is associated with inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). Over 30 genes and multiple IRDs have been reported in association with CLV. However, CLV has not previously been described in macular pattern dystrophies (MPD) in the setting of peripherin-2 (PRPH2) mutations. METHODS: Case Report. RESULTS: We present three unrelated patients who were found to have CLV in the setting of MPD with genetically confirmed variants in PRPH2: c.828 + 3A > T, c.629C > G (p. Pro210Arg), and c.771_772delinsGA (p. Tyr257*). DISCUSSION: These three cases expand the genotypic and phenotypic spectrum of CLV. Patients with PRPH2 variants and MPD should be monitored for development of CLV and its complications, including cystoid macular edema and exudative retinal detachment, to allow early detection and timely management.
42982416.authors: Miltich M, Jung EH, Vidaurri-Martinez J et al.
42982416.title: Coats-like vasculopathy in the setting of PRPH2-associated multifocal macular pattern dystrophy.

42986169.abstract: PURPOSE: Ellipsoid zone (EZ) loss on optical coherence tomography (OCT) correlates with diminished sensitivity on static perimetry (SP). We explore a topographical overlay analysis in USH2A-related retinitis pigmentosa (RP) to develop novel endpoints of structural and functional change. METHODS: Subjects (N = 105) had SP (3× baseline; once annually for 4 years) and annual OCT. B-scans were segmented to outline the EZ. Overlays used visual field modeling and analysis (VFMA) software to superimpose the hill of vision (HOV) onto the en face infrared (IR) fundus image with EZ contours segmented from OCT volume scans. EZ border and three ribbons straddling the EZ border were ray cast onto the HOV. The HOV volume, HOV slope, mean sensitivity (MS), and peak sensitivity were measured. Mixed effect models were used to estimate change rates. RESULTS: Significant decrease over 4 years was found in all measures within the EZ, except slope and peak sensitivity. MS decreased for all ribbons, with outer ribbons showing greater progression than inner ribbons. Inner ribbons had larger decreases in volume and slope than outer ribbons. CONCLUSIONS: SP-OCT overlay analysis showed faster loss of sensitivity outside the EZ margin. The widest ribbon outside the EZ showed greatest progression, suggesting more rapid vision loss occurring distal to the EZ margin. Slope progressed most within the widest inner ribbon, which could mean that slope change is a precursor to EZ loss. TRANSLATIONAL RELEVANCE: This research explores novel endpoints and concepts to characterize the disease progression in USH2A-related RP using imaging and functional overlay techniques.
42986169.authors: Miller AK, Duncan JL, Maguire MG et al.
42986169.title: Static Perimetry-OCT Topographical Overlay Findings in the RUSH2A Study.

42986575.abstract: PURPOSE: To describe the clinical, imaging, and genetic features of non-syndromic neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL)-associated retinal degeneration in a multi-ethnic Asian cohort, with particular emphasis on cases that were initially considered in the differential diagnosis of non-neoplastic uveitis masquerade syndromes. METHODS: This retrospective case series reviewed seven unrelated Singaporean patients (Chinese and Indian ancestry) with genetically confirmed CLN-associated inherited retinal degeneration. Clinical presentation, inflammatory features, longitudinal multimodal imaging, electrophysiology, and molecular findings were analyzed. RESULTS: Symptom onset ranged from 18 to 54 years. Presenting symptoms included "blurred vision/floaters (n = 3)", "nyctalopia (n = 3)", and "hemeralopia (n = 1)". Five patients presented with active ocular inflammation, such as anterior chamber and vitreous cells and retinal vasculitis. Notably, the other two patients (harboring CLN2 and CLN3 variants) did not show overt anterior or posterior segment inflammation; however, their striking structural and imaging similarities to inflammatory retinopathies prompted their inclusion in the masquerade differential. Across all seven patients, serial optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed relentless outer retinal atrophy and loss of the ellipsoid zone. One of the five patients received corticosteroid and immunosuppressive therapy but showed only a limited response, whereas the remaining four patients responded favourably to topical, periocular, or oral corticosteroids. During a follow-up of 2.7-33.1 years, median best-corrected visual acuity declined to logMAR 1.90. Systemic health remained stable without neurological symptoms, except for one CLN2-associated case developing adult-onset neurosensory hearing loss. Pathogenic variants in CLN1, CLN2, CLN3, CLN5, and CLN7 were identified through genetic testing. CLN-associated disease accounted for 1.1% of the inherited retinal disease families in the cohort. CONCLUSIONS: Retinal degeneration associated with CLN1, CLN5, and CLN7 variants frequently presented with intraocular inflammation (ranging from anterior to panuveitis) in our cohort. Yet even patients without obvious inflammatory signs experienced a relentless retinal decline that closely mimicked the structural damage seen in severe posterior uveitis. These findings highlight why early genetic testing is so crucial when working up atypical, symmetrical posterior uveitis or suspected masquerade syndromes.
42986575.authors: Sanjay S, Chee SP, Tang RWC et al.
42986575.journal: Journal of ophthalmic inflammation and infection
42986575.title: Inflammatory masquerade features in adult-onset CLN-associated retinal degeneration in a multiethnic Asian cohort.

42987996.title: Comment on: Impact of Zonular Laxity on the Accuracy of Intraocular Lens Power Calculation Formulas in Cataract Patients With Retinitis Pigmentosa.

42990930.authors: Negueruela S, Di Guida M, Brandi P et al.
42990930.title: Single-cell transcriptome analysis highlights conserved transcriptional responses across multiple models of Retinitis Pigmentosa.

42993231.authors: Sharma A, Wu L, Bloom S et al.
42993231.title: RWC Update: Managing Inherited Retinal Diseases in 2026: Where Are We Now?; Acute Optic Nerve Avulsion With Secondary Central Retinal Artery Occlusion.

42995293.abstract: Subretinal injection procedures for inherited retinal diseases rely on both the instantaneous and long-term mechanical response of the retina, yet a predictive and experimentally validated constitutive framework is still lacking due to experimental and modeling challenges. In this study, we establish a combined experimental-computational approach to characterize and model the viscous-elastic behavior of porcine retina under biaxial loading conditions representative of surgery. Disc-shaped porcine retinal specimens are tested using a small punch, and two complementary protocols (i. e., a multi-ramp stress relaxation and a strain-rate-dependent cyclic loading) are employed. The experiments reveal a pronounced time-dependent behavior that cannot be described by a purely elastic response. To capture this experimental observation, we adopted an inverse finite element approach to identify constitutive parameters of a chosen visco-hyperelastic model, enabling a consistent identification of time-dependent material parameters under biaxial loading conditions. The retina is described as a Neo-Hookean solid augmented with a Prony-series-based viscous-elastic formulation with an elastic and two Maxwell branches. The calibrated model reproduces the full set of experimental responses, including stress relaxation and strain-rate sensitivity. The proposed framework provides a predictive constitutive description of retinal tissue, enabling physiologically relevant simulations of subretinal injection and supporting mechanically informed preoperative planning and device design, and providing a framework for modeling time-dependent behavior of soft hydrated tissues under complex loading conditions.
42995293.authors: Bertolo D, Berti F, Pandolfi A et al.
42995293.title: Experimental-numerical characterization of the time-dependent behavior of the porcine retina.

43000196.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The clinical consequences of ocular trauma in patients with inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) are poorly characterized. This study describes the characteristics, management, and outcomes of ocular trauma in IRD patients. METHODS: A multicenter retrospective case series was conducted across four tertiary ophthalmic centers. Medical records were reviewed to identify patients with genetically confirmed Stargardt disease/ABCA4-associated retinopathy, X-linked retinoschisis (XLRS), PRPH2-associated retinopathy, or pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) who sustained documented ocular trauma. Demographic characteristics, mechanism of injury, ocular findings, visual acuity outcomes, and follow-up data were collected. RESULTS: Sixteen eyes of thirteen patients were included encompassing Stargardt disease (53.8%), Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (30.8%), X-linked retinoschisis (7.7%) and PRPH2-associated retinopathy (7.7%). Mean age at trauma was 19.8 ± 10.4 years, and 92.3% were male. Mean follow-up was 30.6 ± 45.2 months. Sports-related injuries accounted for 69.2% of events, with soccer ball injuries in one-third. No patient was wearing protective eyewear. The most common trauma-related complications included commotio retinae (43.8%) and retinal hemorrhage (25.0%). Commotio retinae developed in 70% of Stargardt-related eyes. Subretinal fibrosis developed in 62.5% of all eyes (10/16). CONCLUSION: Blunt ocular trauma in IRD patients may result in significant retinal complications. Sports-related injuries were the predominant mechanism, highlighting the potential importance of protective eyewear and injury-prevention counseling in this vulnerable population.
43000196.authors: Farrell LC, Muste JC, Tekin D et al.
43000196.title: The effects of blunt ocular trauma in patients with inherited retinal disease: a multicenter case series.

43003402.abstract: BACKGROUND: Choroideremia is an X-linked retinal dystrophy in which female carriers are typically asymptomatic or exhibit only mild peripheral pigmentary changes. CASE PRESENTATION: We report a rare case of scarred choroidal neovascularization (CNV) in a 16-year-old female carrier with genetically confirmed CHM (c.819 + 1 G > C) mutation. The patient first presented at age 12 with unilateral visual decline (20/80) in the right eye. Fundus examination in the right eye demonstrated diffuse pigmentary alterations and central macular fibrosis. Four years later, visual acuity deteriorated to 20/250. Imaging showed subretinal hyperreflective material and established subretinal fibrosis consistent with a scarred neovascular membrane, without active exudation. CONCLUSION: Although severe phenotypes have been described in female carriers, CNVs have been reported across both pediatric and adult males, whereas reports in females to date have been limited to adults. Presentation during adolescence, already at a fibrotic and vision-limiting stage, is exceedingly uncommon. This case highlights the importance of careful screening and close follow-up of at-risk female relatives to enable timely detection and intervention.
43003402.authors: Barayev E, Dotan G, Sternfeld A et al.
43003402.title: Choroidal neovascularization in a 16-year-old female carrier of a CHM mutation.

43004752.abstract: PURPOSE: TTLL5‑related retinopathy, a rare form of autosomal recessive inherited retinal dystrophy, has been mostly documented in adults and as a cone-dominant disorder. This report highlights the phenotype in 2 affected children. METHODS: Retrospective case series of 2 affected siblings and their affected mother (pseudodominant nuclear family). RESULTS: Two Emirati sisters, 17 and 14 years old and from a first-cousin marriage, were evaluated for unexplained reduced vision despite grossly normal fundus exam since approximately 8 years of age and a suspicion for functional visual loss. Fundus examination was significant for areas of tapetal retinal sheen in both. Electroretinography revealed cone-rod dysfunction in the 17-year-old and cone dysfunction in the 14-year-old. Their mother, 61 years old, had bilateral macular atrophy and poor vision since childhood. Exome sequencing the older sister identified a homozygous TTLL5 deletion (encompassing exons 16-26) and segregation analysis confirmed it to be present in homozygosity in the younger sister and mother. This TTLL5 deletion is absent from major variant databases but has been previously reported in homozygosity in another Emirati patient with cone-rod dystrophy. CONCLUSIONS: TTLL5-related retinopathy can be mistaken for functional visual loss or amblyopia in children, leading to delayed diagnosis. A tapetal retinal sheen seems recurrent. This rare homozygous TTLL5 deletion has been previously reported in a different Emirati patient with cone-rod dystrophy and may represent a founder effect in the population.
43004752.title: Pediatric TTLL5-related retinopathy and a recurrent deletion in the United Arab Emirates.

43010769.abstract: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a genetically heterogeneous retinal degenerative disease caused by the progressive loss of photoreceptor cells and atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, which eventually leads to bilateral blindness. As an emerging pan-gene therapeutic approach, optogenetic therapy holds the potential to restore visual function by introducing exogenous photosensitive protein genes into non-photoreceptive retinal neurons. However, the high heterogeneity of RP phenotypes and pathogenic genes causes significant differences in therapeutic benefits among patients treated with optogenetic therapy. This article systematically analyzes the key factors influencing the efficacy of optogenetic therapy for RP from multiple dimensions, including the type and status of target cells, immune responses to adeno-associated virus, ocular complications of advanced RP, administration routes and intervention time windows. It aims to provide a theoretical foundation and practical reference for optimizing the clinical application of optogenetic therapy. 视网膜色素变性（RP）是一种由光感受器细胞进行性死亡和视网膜色素上皮萎缩引起的遗传异质性视网膜退行性疾病，最终导致双眼失明。光遗传治疗作为一种新兴的泛基因疗法，通过将外源性光敏蛋白基因导入视网膜非感光神经元，发挥视功能恢复潜力。然而，RP表型和致病基因的高度异质性导致不同患者接受光遗传治疗后的获益程度存在明显差异。本文从靶细胞的类型及状态、腺相关病毒免疫反应、晚期RP眼部并发症、给药途径、干预时间窗等多个维度，系统剖析影响光遗传治疗RP效果的关键因素，以期为提高光遗传治疗的临床应用水平提供理论依据和实践参考。.
43010769.authors: Lu PR, Han X, Zhu ZQ
43010769.journal: [Zhonghua yan ke za zhi] Chinese journal of ophthalmology
43010769.title: [The key factors affecting the efficacy of optogenetic therapy for retinitis pigmentosa].

43014503.abstract: Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) and the broader "AZOOR complex" have historically encompassed several disorders sharing acute visual symptoms and outer retinal dysfunction. Advances in multimodal imaging have revealed structural abnormalities in many of these presentations, challenging the original concept of an "occult" retinopathy without a visible anatomical correlate. We therefore revisit these concepts in light of modern imaging and current understanding of outer retinal disease. A systematic reassessment of 207 eligible published cases showed that 188 (90.8%) could be assigned a more specific contemporary diagnostic category based on the information available in the original reports. The most frequent assignments were multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS), acute outer retinopathy (AOR), and multizonal outer retinopathy and retinal pigment epitheliopathy (MORR). These findings do not establish that the original diagnoses were incorrect or that each contemporary diagnosis represents a biologically independent disease, but show that many presentations historically grouped under AZOOR can now be characterized more specifically. We review the clinical features, multimodal imaging findings, natural history, and management of the principal retinal entities identified through this reassessment. We also examine inherited, toxic, autoimmune, paraneoplastic, post-infectious, and other disorders that may produce similar retinal appearances or provide the underlying clinical or etiological setting for these presentations. Rather than proposing a new disease classification, we suggest a pattern-based diagnostic approach in which OCT and fundus autofluorescence form the core imaging assessment, with additional imaging modalities selected according to the clinical presentation and differential diagnosis. Imaging is used to characterize the predominant pattern and anatomical level of retinal injury and, when possible, to identify a more specific retinal diagnosis; clinical history, systemic evaluation, laboratory testing, electrophysiology, and genetic testing can then guide further investigation of its etiological setting or identify a specific alternative diagnosis. This approach allows patients presenting within the broad clinical spectrum historically associated with AZOOR to be characterized at the most specific level supported by contemporary imaging, while recognizing that the biological relationships among these retinal entities remain incompletely understood.
43014503.authors: Ramtohul P, Fouad Y, Bianco L et al.
43014503.journal: Progress in retinal and eye research
43014503.title: Acute Zonal Occult Outer Retinopathy: Reappraising a Historical Clinical Concept in the Era of Multimodal Imaging.

43018415.abstract: PURPOSE: Variable expressivity is well recognized in autosomal-dominant inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) but is increasingly observed and less well defined in recessive IRDs. Despite the traditional view of recessive IRDs as monogenic disorders with high penetrance, phenotypic differences among individuals sharing identical biallelic variants suggest additional disease modifiers. We quantified genotype-phenotype concordance in EYS- and USH2A-associated retinitis pigmentosa (RP) and characterized phenotypic variability among individuals with identical primary genotypes. METHODS: Participants underwent standardized ophthalmic assessment with multimodal imaging. Longitudinal ellipsoid zone (EZ) widths were measured from optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans obtained ≥12 months apart. Baseline EZ width and age at OCT assessment were compared among individuals sharing identical primary genotypes. Genotype-matched comparisons in which younger individuals demonstrated smaller EZ widths than older counterparts were classified as age-discordant structural comparisons. RESULTS: Ninety patients (41 EYS, 49 USH2A) were included. Recurrent variants EYS c.6416G>A (p.Cys2139Tyr) and USH2A c.2802T>G (p.Cys934Trp) were identified in 46% and 35% of probands, respectively. Females showed greater baseline EZ preservation, although differences were not statistically significant. Marked variability was observed within matched genotypes. Several genotype-matched comparisons demonstrated age-discordant structural variability, including younger individuals with substantially smaller EZ widths than older genotype-matched counterparts. In EYS-associated disease, the largest discordant comparison demonstrated 85.4% less EZ preservation in the younger individuals despite younger age, and the corresponding value in USH2A-associated disease was 81.8%. Intrafamilial discordance further supported the possibility of modifying influences beyond the primary genotype. CONCLUSIONS: Disease severity varied substantially among individuals sharing identical primary genotypes, supporting contributions from additional genetic or environmental modifiers. TRANSLATIONAL RELEVANCE: Recognition of variability within recessive IRDs has implications for prognosis, trial stratification, and interpretation of treatment response beyond genotype alone.
43018415.authors: Neo JE, Chen JQ, Ngo WK et al.
43018415.title: Phenotypic Variability in Individuals With Genotype-Matched EYS- and USH2A-Associated Autosomal-Recessive Retinitis Pigmentosa.

43018420.abstract: PURPOSE: Several retinal degenerations initiate because of gene defects in the outermost retinal layer, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Subretinal injection achieves optimal RPE transduction but has limitations, including iatrogenic damage. Here, we develop and evaluate the efficacy of a novel adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid with intravitreal delivery, in an effort to overcome limitations of subretinal delivery for treatment of retinal degenerations that require precise targeting of the outer retina. METHODS: We conducted a high-throughput screening of 1.28 × 109 AAV2 capsids, each with a different 7-mer peptide insertion to alter its binding properties, to be delivered with intravitreal (IVT) injection, a less invasive surgical procedure. A novel AAV variant, variant 3 (AAV2.Var3) was found to transduce RPE cells with CAG-GFP and Best1-GFP in mouse eyes. For comparison, a leading, clinical-stage vector that is also AAV2-based, 7m8, effectively transduces the outer retina but has limited success targeting RPE through IVT delivery. To test the therapeutic efficacy of variant 3, we packaged therapeutic gene, hRPE65, and injected it intravitreally in rd12 mice, a disease model for Leber congenital amaurosis type 2. RESULTS: AAV2.Var3-hRPE65 treated mice cohorts showed an increase in RPE65 protein expression and function as well as visual function in response to light flashes. Translatability of AAV2.Var3 for intravitreal gene delivery was validated by AAV2.Var3-Best1-GFP vector induced expression of GFP in peripheral RPE cells in non-human primate macaque. CONCLUSIONS: Variant 3 is capable of RPE transduction with IVT injection, serving as a vehicle for less invasive IVT gene delivery to the RPE. Therapeutic gene delivery leads to functional results with efficiency limitations.
43018420.authors: Singh S, Visel M, Byrne LC et al.
43018420.title: Discovering a Novel AAV2-Based Capsid for RPE Transduction Via Intravitreal Injection for Leber Congenital Amaurosis Type 2 Gene Therapy.

43018422.abstract: PURPOSE: While variants in RHO are a leading cause of autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (RP), the c.647T>A p.(Met216Lys) variant gives rise to a phenotype that can mimic choroideremia. We describe its long-term natural history. METHODS: Patients were included from four centers (in France, the United Kingdom, and the United States). Clinical features analyzed included pedigrees, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), visual fields, color vision, electroretinography, and multimodal imaging (color fundus photography, short-wavelength and near-infrared fundus autofluorescence [SW- and NIR-AF], and spectral domain optical coherence tomography [SD-OCT]). RESULTS: Seventeen patients (11 women; median age at first examination, 45 years [range, 13-68 years]) from eight unrelated families were included. Follow-up was available for 13 individuals (median, 159 months [range, 24-286 months]). Impaired night vision was the predominant presenting symptom (71%), with BCVA relatively preserved at baseline. Visual fields showed pericentral round scotomas, enlarging and coalescing over time, with relative sparing of the far periphery. On SW-AF, younger patients showed a diffuse granular pattern, whereas older patients showed well-demarcated patches of autofluorescence loss. Serial imaging in seven patients confirmed that these patches enlarged and coalesced within individuals over time. Color fundus photography showed preserved optic disc color and normal retinal vessel caliber. SD-OCT demonstrated outer retinal tubulations, a thinned choroid, and progressive ellipsoid zone (EZ) loss (median rate of EZ width loss, 176 µm per year). CONCLUSIONS: The RHO c.647T>A p.(Met216Lys) variant is associated with a slowly progressive, unusual chorioretinal dystrophy phenotype that can closely mimic choroideremia. Our findings suggest pathogenetic mechanisms that differ from typical RHO-associated RP.
43018422.authors: Hallali G, Martin-Gutierrez MP, Ba-Abbad R et al.
43018422.title: Natural History of an Unusual Chorioretinal Phenotype Associated With the RHO p.(Met216Lys) Variant.

43019019.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hearing loss (HL) is a genetically and clinically heterogeneous sensorineural disorder. The World Health Organization estimates that ∼1.5 billion people worldwide currently live with some degree of HL (all causes and severities combined), a burden projected to rise to 2.5 billion by 2050. A substantial proportion of early-onset and congenital HL is attributable to genetic causes, particularly in populations with a high rate of consanguinity, such as Pakistan, where consanguinity increases the prevalence of autosomal recessive disorders and thereby enriches the genetic landscape of hereditary HL. METHODS: In this study, two consanguineous families (HL-76 and HL-79) presenting with HL and vision impairment as phenotypes were ascertained from the province of Balochistan, Pakistan. RESULTS: Exome sequencing (ES) followed by Sanger sequencing revealed cosegregation of MYO7A variants c.487G > A p.(Gly163Arg) and c.4079A > G p.(Asp1360Gly) in families HL-79 and HL-76, respectively. Bi-allelic variants in MYO7A are known to cause Usher syndrome type 1, characterized by deafness, progressive vision loss, and vestibular areflexia. The variants identified in our cohort were predicted to be damaging by in silico analysis. CONCLUSION: The p.(Asp1360Gly) variant identified in family HL-76 represents a potentially novel contribution to the MYO7A mutational spectrum, whereas p.(Gly163Arg) identified in family HL-79 is a recurrent variant previously classified as pathogenic/likely pathogenic in ClinVar and in prior published reports. Together, these findings establish a molecular diagnosis for both families, with direct implications for genetic counseling and clinical management.
43019019.authors: Durrani S, Tariq N, Ishaq R et al.
43019019.title: Identification of MYO7A Variants in Consanguineous Pakistani Families with Syndromic Hearing Loss.

43020825.abstract: X-linked Retinitis Pigmentosa (XLRP) is an inherited retinopathy predominantly caused by RPGR mutations, ultimately leading to photoreceptor apoptosis and vision loss. Although the genetic basis is well established, the downstream pathogenic and molecular mechanisms remain inadequately elucidated. The aim of this study is to explore the pathogenesis from the perspective of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, which was previously underexplored. Using rd9 mouse retinas and mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cells, we confirmed the presence of ER stress, activation of the unfolded protein response (UPR), and photoreceptor apoptosis through Western blot and immunofluorescence (IF) analyses. Furthermore, knockdown of Cryaa in 661W cells directly induced ER stress and UPR activation. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) photomicrographs revealed significant ultrastructural alterations in ER and mitochondria within rd9 retinas and MEF cells. Proteomic analyses of rd9 retinas identified significantly enriched pathways including UPR, protein folding, and unfolded protein binding, associated with Cryaa downregulation. Collectively, our results identify Cryaa as a critical regulator of ER stress and demonstrate that its reduction promotes UPR activation and subsequent photoreceptor apoptosis in the rd9 model. These findings reveal, for the first time, a key role for Cryaa in XLRP pathology and may provide a novel therapeutic perspective for this disease.
43020825.authors: Yang M, Qiu R, Yao S et al.
43020825.title: Activation of ER stress mediated by HspB4/Cryaa reduction contributes to photoreceptor apoptosis in rd9 mouse model of X-linked Retinitis Pigmentosa.

43021544.abstract: Inherited retinal diseases (IRDs) are a heterogeneous group of genetic disorders that cause progressive vision loss. A subset of IRDs is associated with ubiquitously expressed genes involved in fundamental cellular processes, often resulting in multisystem disease. Among these is Zellweger spectrum disorder (ZSD), caused by pathogenic variants in PEX genes required for peroxisome biogenesis and function. There are no proven targeted disease-modifying treatments for ZSD, and it is unclear whether localized restoration of peroxisome function is sufficient to mitigate retinal degeneration. We previously demonstrated that HsPEX1 retinal gene augmentation therapy in a mouse model of mild ZSD homozygous for the murine equivalent (PEX1-p.[Gly844Asp]) of the most common deleterious allele in patients (PEX1-c.[2528G>A], PEX1-p.[Gly843Asp]), improved retinal electrophysiological response. Here, we present a comprehensive, dose-range evaluation of a re-designed, clinically relevant AAV8-delivered HsPEX1 subretinal gene therapy, employing expanded outcome measures. We observed a significant improvement in functional vision, retinal response, photoreceptor structure, retinal pigment epithelium integrity, subretinal inflammation, and peroxisomal metabolites, durable to the endpoint of 6 months post single subretinal injection. These studies provide preclinical proof-of-concept that localized retinal gene replacement can mitigate vision loss in peroxisome-mediated IRD.
43021544.authors: Omri S, Di Pietro E, McDougald DS et al.
43021544.journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
43021544.title: Clinically relevant AAV8-PEX1 gene therapy preserves retinal integrity and function long-term in a murine model of Zellweger spectrum disorder.

43022838.abstract: A definitive molecular diagnosis is essential for the clinical management of rare genetic diseases (RGDs), guiding prognosis, genetic counseling, and therapeutic development. RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as promising strategies for RGDs owing to their ability to modulate gene expression and splicing. Here, we establish an integrated and scalable pipeline from variant discovery to RNA-based therapy in inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). Genome sequencing identified three cryptic variants in known IRD genes. Two novel deep intronic variants in SDCCAG8 were characterized by RT-PCR to induce pseudoexon inclusion. In addition, a previously described deep intronic variant in CEP290 was detected and reproduced on patient-derived fibroblasts, confirming aberrant splicing. A third family carrying the recurrent ABCA4 c.768G>T silent variant was included to corroborate the translational strength of our pipeline and to provide an additional model for RNA-based therapeutic correction. We designed and tested 16 splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides (ssASOs) in patient-derived fibroblasts, HeLa cells transfected with mutant minigenes, and, when available, human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal organoids. For each variant, at least one ssASO successfully improved normal splicing and increased gene expression in patient-derived models. Overall, this study validates an innovative end-to-end translational workflow and highlights how molecular diagnosis can directly drive the development of personalized RNA-based therapies.
43022838.authors: Zadorozhna M, Rossi S, Tenderini E et al.
43022838.title: Targeting cryptic splicing variants in SDCCAG8, CEP290, and ABCA4: A translational workflow from diagnosis to ASO-based therapy.

NCT00000114.eligibility_text: Men and nonpregnant women between ages 18 and 49 years with common forms of RP were included. All eligible patients had retinal arteriolar attenuation, elevated dark adaptation thresholds, and reduced ERGs. Patients had best corrected Snellen visual acuity of 20/100 or better, central visual field diameter on the Goldman perimeter with V4 e white test light of 8 degrees or greater, and ERG amplitude of 2.5 or greater in response to 0.5-Hz white light or of 0.12 ultraviolet light or greater in response to 30-Hz white flickering light in at least one eye. In addition, patients had normal fasting serum retinol and serum liver function profile and weight above the lower fifth percentile for age, sex, and height. All patients had a total estimated pre-trial intake of vitamins A and E from diet plus pills not greater than 11,500 IU/day and 40 IU/day, respectively.
NCT00000114.summary: To determine whether supplements of vitamin A or vitamin E alone or in combination affect the course of retinitis pigmentosa.

INCLUSION CRITERIA:

Patients must have hyperornithemia and a deficiency of OAT activity to enter the study.
NCT00001166.lead: Gyrate Atrophy of the Choroid and Retina
NCT00001166.official_title: The Diagnosis, Pathogenesis and Treatment of Gyrate Atrophy of the Choroid and Retina
NCT00001166.summary:
Gyrate atrophy is a rare hereditary disease of the eye's retina (the layer of light-sensitive tissue that lines the inside of the eyeball) and choroid (a vascular layer of tissue behind the retina). Degeneration of these structures causes near-sightedness, cataracts and progressive loss of vision. This study will examine eye function and chemical and molecular abnormalities in patients with gyrate atrophy to try to better understand, diagnose, and treat the condition. Patients with other degenerative diseases of the choroid and retina, such as retinitis pigmentosa, choroideremia, and others, will also be studied for comparison. Family members of patients will be studied, when possible, to try to identify the genetic basis of the disease and gain information that will aid in genetic counseling.

Study participants will undergo a physical examination and eye examination, including tests of color vision, field of vision, and ability to see in the dark. An electroretinogram and electrooculogram will measure visual cell function. Photographs of the retina will be taken. Blood will be drawn for biochemical study and gene research. Family members who agree to participate in the study will undergo the same eye tests and will also have blood drawn for genetic studies. Patients with gyrate atrophy will also be asked to undergo a small skin biopsy for biochemical and genetic study. They will provide a family history in order to draw a family tree showing how the disease is distributed among family members.

Patients with gyrate atrophy may also participate in studies of the effect of vitamin B6 and diet on blood levels of the amino acid ornithine, which is elevated in patients with gyrate atrophy. Participants will take 500 mg of vitamin B6 by mouth every day for 3 to 6 months. If this study confirms a reduction of ornithine levels, then long-term studies of the vitamin as a possible treatment for the disease may be started.

After the vitamin B6 study, patients will start a nearly protein-free diet to lower ornithine blood levels. More than 2,000 calories are carbohydrate and fat. Some special low-protein foods and limited fruit is included, plus amino acid supplements. Patients who have carefully adhered to this diet have lowered their ornithine levels and slowed disease progression. Patients will be hospitalized for the first 1 to 3 weeks for close monitoring with frequent urine and blood tests. When the blood ornithine level is normalized, a less restricted low protein diet will be prescribed. Participants will have monthly blood tests and a complete eye examination every 6 months to 1 year to evaluate disease progression.
NCT00001166.title: Gyrate Atrophy of the Choroid and Retina

NCT00001347.eligibility_text:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Patients must have documentation of neurosensory hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa and fulfill the clinical characteristics (Table) as accepted for USH 1 and USH 2.
* The minimal test battery will identify all patients with USH 1 and USH 2 as well as possible subtypes.
* Candidates will be recruited from lists of patients willing to participate in research studies compiled by the R.P. Foundation, and by referral from their private physicians.
* On occasion additional family members will be studied after an initial individual is ascertained as above.
* No patients with intrauterine and childhood infections, and intrauterine and birth complications can result in trauma to both the auditory or visual system and a positive history for these conditions will necessitate exclusion from the study.
NCT00001347.lead: Study of Usher Syndromes, Type 1 and Type 2
NCT00001347.official_title: Usher Syndrome - Clinical and Molecular Studies
NCT00001347.summary:
The purpose of this investigation is to gain additional knowledge about what causes type 1 and type 2 Usher syndrome-inherited diseases that can cause balance problems and impaired hearing and vision-and to develop better diagnostic tests. Patients with type 1 Usher syndrome usually are deaf from birth and have speech and balance problems. Patients with type 2 disease generally are hearing impaired but have no balance problems. All patients develop eye problems that cause difficulty seeing in the dark.

The development of newer and more sophisticated diagnostic tests may detect subtle differences in signs and symptoms that allow more accurate distinction between the two types of Usher syndrome. This study will use these tests to classify these syndromes and eventually identify the genes responsible for them.

Study participants will have a medical and family history taken and a family tree constructed. They will undergo a thorough eye examination, including special tests of color vision, field of vision, and ability to see in the dark. An electroretinogram will be done to measure the function of cells in the retina, and a procedure called fluorescein angiography will be done to look at and photograph the blood vessels in the retina. Special hearing and balance tests will also done. Hearing tests include physical examination of the ears and wearing earphones while listening to tones. Balance and coordination tests require tasks such as walking in a straight line and standing in the dark with eyes closed. A caloric stimulation test will also be done, in which a small amount of water is irrigated into the ear canal. For gene studies, blood samples will be collected from patients and all available family members.
NCT00001347.title: Study of Usher Syndromes, Type 1 and Type 2

NCT00004574.summary:
This study will determine whether short term intravenous infusion of vitamins A and E in patients with abetalipoproteinemia can reverse disease symptoms in these patients. Abetalipoproteinemia is an inherited metabolic defect that prevents fat-soluble vitamins, such as A and E, from being absorbed from the intestines into the bloodstream and from being secreted by the liver. The deficiencies of vitamins A and E can result in severe vision impairment and a gait disorder. Treatment with megadoses of these vitamins, taken by mouth, may delay or arrest symptoms, but many continue to progress.

For this study, a single patient with moderately severe eye and neurological defects will be given essential fatty acids and fat soluble vitamins directly through a vein (intravenously) using FDA-approved replacements with a fat emulsion and multivitamins containing fat-soluble vitamins. This route of administration will bypass the digestive tract, where the absorption problem occurs. The infusions will be given twice a week for one month and then weekly for another month. Blood tests will be done weekly to measure blood lipids (fatty acids and other substances), cell counts, and vitamin levels. Eye and neurological examinations will be done once a month.
NCT00004574.title: Vitamin Replacement in Abetalipoproteinemia

NCT00016471.eligibility_text:
Inclusion criteria:

Any Ashkenazi Jewish individual with combined hearing and visual loss that is or may be any type of Usher syndrome, or a family member of said individual.

Exclusion criteria:

Any individual who is not an Ashkenazi Jew or does not have combined hearing and visual loss or whose disease has been previously determined not to be Usher syndrome.
NCT00016471.official_title: A Genetic Analysis of Usher Syndrome in Ashkenazi Jews
NCT00016471.summary:
Hearing loss and loss of vision can be very harmful to the well-being and life of people who suffer from them. Usher syndrome is the name of a disease where people have both hearing loss and visual loss. In fact more than half of people who are deaf and blind have Usher syndrome. In this study we are trying to find the causes of all types of Usher syndrome and to learn more about how the eyes and ears work. Usher syndrome is caused by changes in our genes that lead to mistakes in the functioning of our eyes and ears.

We may conduct hearing tests called audiograms to test hearing and a vision test called an electroretinogram (ERG) to test how well the retina (the part of your eye that senses light) is working on participants in the study. From these tests we can tell what kind of Usher syndrome a participant may have.

We will then get DNA from participants by drawing blood. The DNA will be studied, along with DNA from members of the participant's family and other families, to try to find the gene that is causing Usher syndrome in the participant.

Once the gene is found we will be able to study it to learn more about how the eyes and ears work.

If a subject has already been diagnosed we may just need copies of their medical records and blood can be drawn locally.

In order to increase the power of the study and the likelihood of detecting relevant genes participants will be taken from the Ashkenazi Jewish population group only. This will make it much easier to find the genes.
NCT00016471.title: A Genetic Analysis of Usher Syndrome in Ashkenazi Jews

NCT00063765.official_title: A Phase I Study of NT-501-10 and NT-501-6A.02, Implants of Encapsulated Human NTC-210 Cells Releasing Ciliary Neurotrophic Factor (CNTF), in Patients With Retinitis Pigmentosa
NCT00063765.summary:
This study will evaluate the safety of a ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) implant placed in the eye to allow the release of CNTF directly on the retina. The results of this study may lead to a larger investigation of CNTF implants to treat retinitis pigmentosa (RP), a progressive degenerative eye disease that begins with loss of peripheral vision and night blindness and often leads to blindness in later life.

Currently, there are no effective treatments for RP. Researchers have found, however, that certain proteins, called ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), can partially protect cells in the eye if given directly inside the eye. A major challenge in treating RP is to deliver medicine directly into the eye. One way to ensure that CNTF gets into the eye is to surgically place an implant inside the eye to release the protein.

Patients 18 years of age and older with retinitis pigmentosa whose visual acuity is 20/100 or worse may be eligible for this study. Candidates will be screened with a medical history, physical examination, eye examinations, and eye photographs. The eye examination includes measurement of visual acuity and eye pressure, examination of the pupils and eye movements, and examination of the lens and back of the eye. In addition, patients will have the following tests:

* Visual field test: Patients look at a central spot on a white screen and tell the examiner whenever they see a small light appear at other places on the screen.
* Electroretinogram (ERG): Electrodes are taped to the patient's forehead. Special contact lenses are placed on the eyes, similar to normal contact lenses, after the eye has been numbed with drops. The contact lenses sense small electrical signals generated by the retina. The ERG measures the electrical activity of the retina when it is stimulated by light. For the ERG recording, the patient looks inside a large, hollow, dark sphere, and sees flashes of light, first in the dark, and then with a light turned on in the sphere.
* Optical coherence tomography: This test, done with the machine used to examine the eye, measures retinal thickness by producing cross-sectional pictures of the retina.

Participants undergo surgery at the NIH Clinical Center in a 30-minute operation to place the implant in one eye. The surgery is done under local anesthetic. Before the procedure, patients are given a steroid injection along side the eye to minimize inflammation after surgery. Following the procedure, patients return for follow-up visits once a month for 6 months. At these visits, several of the exams described above are repeated to evaluate treatment effects and check for adverse side effects. After 6 months, the implant is surgically removed. Post-surgical care for both implant and explant surgeries include examinations the day and week after surgery to examine the wound, a high dose of steroid immediately after surgery, oral antibiotics for 7 days, and eye drops for 1 week to prevent infection and inflammation.
NCT00063765.title: Evaluation of Safety of Ciliary Neurotrophic Factor Implants in the Eye

NCT00065455.official_title: Pilot Study on the Effect of Vitamin A Supplementation on Cone Function in Retinitis Pigmentosa
NCT00065455.summary: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a collective term for a group of inherited retinal dystrophies that are a major cause of irreversible blindness. RP of some type occurs in approximately 1 out of 3500 persons in the United States(1). Gene mutations are responsible for the majority of RP. To date, mutations have been identified in 30 different genes linked to RP(2). The visual prognosis of RP is poor, since the gradual but relentless visual field loss leads eventually to some degree of blindness(3). Although no effective treatment for RP has been identified, participants supplemented with a daily oral dose of 15,000 IU vitamin A palmitate have shown, on average, a slower rate of deterioration of retinal function when the intervention is continued over several years(4). The purpose of this research is to determine whether administration of high oral doses of vitamin A can acutely improve cone photoreceptor function in RP participants as measured by electroretinography (ERG). In this interventional, non-randomized, prospective, pilot study, 5 participants will receive a daily oral dose of 50,000 IU of vitamin A palmitate for 4 weeks, followed by a maintenance dose of 15,000 IU daily for the subsequent 2 weeks. The primary efficacy outcome is a relative percentage change in ERG response amplitude subsequent to vitamin A supplementation. A secondary efficacy outcome is a relative percentage change in implicit time from pre- to post- vitamin A supplementation, with improvement specified as a shorter response implicit time. Other secondary outcomes will be improvements in visual field (Humphery, 10-2; sum of thresholds). Safety outcomes include visual fields, ETDRS visual acuity, intraocular pressure, serum vitamin A level and liver function tests.

NCT00100230.official_title: Investigation of Effectiveness and Safety of High Dose Docosahexaenoic Acid (DHA) in X-Linked Retinitis Pigmentosa
NCT00100230.summary:
Purpose:

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is characterized by progressive loss of visual function due to specific genetic mutations. This trial is focused on patients with one of the most severe forms of the disease, X-linked inherited RP (XLRP). This disease is characterized by early onset (typically loss of night vision as a child) followed by loss of peripheral vision as a teenager and young adult. There is no male-to-male transmission of the disease in the family.

There is no cure for RP and treatment options are limited. Two clinical trials have not found a benefit from nutritional supplementation with the long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid, docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), at low daily doses although there is evidence that it slows disease progression in certain instances. In this clinical trial, we propose that a high dose nutritional DHA supplement will slow the loss of visual function and preserve usable vision in patients with XLRP.

This study is a 4-year placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial meaning that patients have a 50-50 chance of receiving placebo or experimental treatment. A total of 66 patients will be enrolled; 33 will receive placebo and 33 will receive the treatment. Entry criteria include diagnosis of XLRP by an ophthalmologist, age 7 to 32 years, male, sufficient visual function such that disease progression can be followed for the entire duration of the trial, and a willingness to visit the testing site (Dallas, TX) once a year.

Annual visual function testing includes ETDRS visual acuity, full-field and multifocal electroretinography (ERG), static peripheral visual fields, and fundus photography. Cone ERG function is the primary outcome measure.

NCT00106743.summary:
This study will explore clinical and genetic aspects of Usher syndrome, an inherited disease causing deafness or impaired hearing, visual problems, and, in some cases, unsteadiness or balance problems. Patients with type 1 Usher syndrome usually are deaf from birth and have speech and balance problems. Patients with type 2 disease generally are hearing impaired but have no balance problems. Patients with type 3 disease have progressive hearing loss and balance problems. All patients develop retinitis pigmentosa, an eye disease that causes poor night vision and eventually, blindness.

Patients of any age with Usher syndrome may be eligible for this study. Patients who have had eye and hearing evaluations are asked to send their medical records to the research team at the National Eye Institute (NEI) for review. They are also asked to have a blood sample drawn by a medical professional and sent to NEI for genetic analysis. Finally, they are interviewed about their family histories, particularly about other relative with eye disease. Patients who have not been evaluated previously have the following tests and procedures at NIH:

* Family medical history, especially regarding eye disease. A family tree is drawn.
* Blood draw for genetic studies of Usher syndrome.
* Eye examination to assess visual acuity and eye pressure, and to examine pupils, lens, retina, and eye movements.
* Electroretinogram (ERG) to test the function of visual cells. Wearing eye patches, the patient sits in a dark room for 30 minutes. Electrodes are taped to the forehead and the eye patches are removed. The surface of the eye is numbed with eye drops and contact lenses are placed on the eyes. The patient looks inside a hollow, dark globe and sees a series of light flashes. Then a light is turned on inside the globe and more flashes appear. The contact lenses sense small electrical signals generated by the retina when the light flashes.
* Fluorescein angiography to evaluate the eye's blood vessels. A yellow dye is injected into an arm vein and travels to the blood vessels in the eyes. Pictures of the retina are taken using a camera that flashes a blue light into the eye. The pictures show if any dye has leaked from the vessels into the retina, indicating possible blood vessel abnormality.
* Hearing tests to help determine the patient's type of Usher syndrome. Tests to evaluate hearing include examination of both ears with an otoscope, evaluation of the middle ear and inner ear, and hearing tests using earphones that deliver tones and words the subject listens and responds to.
* Vestibular testing for balance function. Balance testing involves three procedures:

Videonystagmography: This test records eye movements with little cameras. First the patient follows the movements of some small lights. Next, while wearing goggles, the patient lies on an exam table and turns to the right and left. Lastly, a soft stream of air is blown into the patient's ears four times, once in each ear with cool air and once in each ear with warm air.

Rotary chair test: With electrodes placed on the forehead, the patient sits in a rotary chair in a dark room. Several red lights appear on the wall of the room and the patient follows the lights as they move back and forth. Then the chair turns at several speeds, all slower than a merry-go-round.

Vestibular evoked potential: Electrodes are placed behind the patient's ear and at the base of the neck. Seated in a reclining chair and wearing earphones, the patient hears a brief series of loud clicking sounds. When the sounds are on, the patient is asked to lift his or her head up a few inches from the chair. The electrodes record information from the muscles in the neck as the sounds enter the ear.

NCT00231010.summary:
This multinational study will investigate the inheritance of genetic retinal degeneration in families of different nationalities and ethnic backgrounds in order to identify the genes that, when altered, cause retinal degeneration. The retina is a light-sensitive membrane lining the back part of the eye. It relays vision signals to the brain, which the brain interprets into sight. When the retina degenerates, vision is altered and possibly lost. The findings of this study should help improve diagnosis and methods of treatment for these disorders. Participating institutions include: the National Institutes for Health in Bethesda, Maryland; the University of Miami in Florida; the Casey Eye Institute in Portland, Oregon; the Byrd Health Sciences Center in Morgantown, West Virginia; the University of Texas Southwestern Medical School in Dallas, Texas; the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center in Memphis; the Prasad Eye Institute in Hyderabad, India; National Center of Excellence in Molecular Biology in Lahore, Pakistan; and the Jules Gonin Hospital in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Patients with retinitis pigmentosa and closely related diseases such as Usher syndrome, snowflake vitreoretinal dystrophy and Bietti crystalline dystrophy may be eligible for this study. Participants undergo the following tests and procedures:

* Medical and surgical history, including family history of vision problems.
* Examination to clarify the type of retinal degeneration.
* Eye examination, including tests of color vision, field of vision and ability to see in the dark
* Electroretinogram to test the function of visual cells. For this test, the patient sits in a dark room for 30 minutes with his or her eyes patched. Then, a small electrode (silver disk) is taped to the forehead and the eye patches are removed. The surface the eyes is numbed with eye drops, and contact lenses are placed on the eyes. The patient looks inside a large dark globe that emits a series of light flashes. Then a light is turned on inside the globe and more lights flash. The contact lenses sense small electrical signals generated by the retina when the light flashes.
* Hearing tests for patients with a personal or family history of deafness. Tests include an audiogram, ear examination and test of middle ear function. For middle ear function testing, the patient feels a little air pressure change for a moment and hears some tones. Another test requires the patient to sit quietly with electrodes on the head, forehead and earlobes.
* Balance testing, including walking in a straight line, standing with eyes closed in the dark and other tests of coordination, and caloric testing. For the caloric testing, any ear wax in the ear canal is removed before the test begins. Then, electrodes are placed on the skin near the eyes and on the forehead. A small amount of cool (sometimes cold) or warm water is instilled into each ear canal, first one and then the other.
* Blood sample collection for genetic testing.

NCT00341874.sponsor: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD)
NCT00341874.summary:
Objective: One objective of this study is to genetically map and identify mutated genes for human hereditary hearing loss. A second objective is to study the function of these genes in the auditory system using mouse models. Human hereditary hearing impairment is the result of abnormal ear development, abnormal ear function or both. Although the genes for numerous deafness loci have been mapped and identified, there are still many families segregating deafness as a monogenic trait but a mutant allele can t be ascribed to one of the currently reported deafness genes . In order to map and identify novel mutated genes associated with hearing loss in humans, we will continue to ascertain large families segregating syndromic and nonsyndromic deafness as a monogenic trait.

Study population: This study will ascertain subjects from consanguineous Pakistani families segregating hearing loss consisting of both nonsyndromic and syndromic forms of deafness of genetic etiology. Since a majority of Pakistani marriages are between first cousins, this tends to bring together the same recessive mutations for hearing loss with multiple affected individuals within single family lines, which is an advantage for this genetic study. A few years ago we stopped ascertaining families in India. We continue to ascertain both affected and unaffected Pakistani family members from age 2 years and up. Adults provide informed consent both for themselves and their children who agree to participate in this study. We will ascertain both genders and all Pakistani races and ethnicities.

Design: Subjects will be screened and consented by our collaborating Associate Investigator in Pakistan. After consenting, the subjects will undergo a history and physical, audiological assessment and testing, vestibular assessment and testing, and blood and urine analysis tests, along with a blood sample or buccal swab sample that will be used for genomic DNA extraction. Probands at the time of ascertainment are initially assumed to have a form of nonsyndromic deafness. Additional tests may be performed depending on the history or physical of the individual or after the deafness gene is identified. Data from functional studies in animal models may also point to other concomitant clinical features along with hearing loss. These additional tests may include: photographs or videotapes of a subject s body and face; eye and vision examinations for those with suspected or known eyesight problems related to their genetic hearing loss mutations, and EKGs and/or Echocardiograms for those with suspected or known heart problems related to their genetic hearing loss mutations. Urine and blood analyses may be requested for those individuals with genetic nephritic issues or infertility. For example, when a deaf female individual in a family is subsequently discovered to have Perrault syndrome, a recessive disorder characterized by hearing loss (usually the initial manifestation) and ovarian dysgenesis/primary amenorrhea, additional evaluations would then be conducted for a definitive diagnosis of Perrault syndrome. Such an evaluation would include a pelvic ultrasound scan and measurements of serum estrogen and gonadotropins. Similarly, in some of these families, hearing impaired males may be asked about their fertility since the possibility of male infertility in families segregating Perrault syndrome remains an open question. For genetic analyses, genomic DNA extracted from a blood sample or a buccal swab from affected and unaffected members of families segregating hereditary hearing loss will be genetically screened with polymorphic markers (STRs or SNPs) for linkage to the known deafness loci. The hearing phenotype of children (\>2 years old), adolescent and adult subjects will be assigned on the basis of performance from audiological examinations. Genomic DNA from families where deafness is found to be unlinked to the known deafness loci will then be used in genome wide screens with approximately 950,000 SNP markers distributed across the entire human genome to identify novel deafness loci. Alternatively, DNA samples from affected and unaffected individuals will undergo whole exome sequencing (WES) or whole genome sequencing (WGS) with a focus on potentially pathogenic variants located only in chromosomal regions of markers genetically linked to deafness. Subsequently, novel deafness genes will be positionally identified and their functions studied.

Outcome measures: Novel deafness loci and genes associated with hearing loss will be identified and will provide new insight into mechanisms required for sound transduction in humans. Data from this study is likely to be the basis of commercially available tests for early diagnosis and timely genetic counseling for at risk couples as well as the development of strategies to preserve hearing and prevent hearing loss.

NCT00378742.official_title: National Ophthalmic Genotyping and Phenotyping Network Stage 1 - Creation of DNA Repository for Inherited Ophthalmic Diseases
NCT00378742.summary:
The National Ophthalmic Disease Genotyping and Phenotyping Network (eyeGENE(R)) is a genomic medicine initiative created by the National Eye Institute (NEI), part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH), in partnership with clinics and laboratories across the vision research community. The core mission of eyeGENE(R) is to facilitate research into the causes and mechanisms of rare inherited eye diseases and accelerate pathways to treatments. This study collects DNA samples from patients with inherited eye diseases to facilitate research to identify genetic factors responsible for these conditions. Nearly 500 genes that contribute to inherited eye diseases have been identified. As a result, gene-based therapies are being pursued to treat eye genetic diseases that were once considered untreatable.

Physicians in collaborating institutions will recruit patients to participate in the study. Patients will provide a blood sample and undergo a standard eye examination. The blood sample and clinical information will then be sent to the NEI for testing, processing and storing in the biorepository. Patients are given the option to receive results back and/or to be re-contacted in the event of future clinical studies. Information supplied to the testing laboratories includes a unique identification number, the patient gender, and the patient date of birth. The stored samples are available to researchers along with information about the patient's disease, but without patient identifiers.
NCT00378742.title: Repository for Inherited Eye Diseases
